extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, critics, and literate readers of dramatic art
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative standards for composing and judging English tragedy (verse, style, plot, and performance), with additional social-critique on affectation and authenticity of behaviour/appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation (self-conscious behaviour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation is when consciousness fondly approves a man's own conceptions and betrays itself in gesture and behaviour; it makes wit into deformity and beauty into disfigurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not posture, twist into artificial attitudes, or alter countenance and gesture to solicit admiration; keep attention fixed on the main design of life or on the chief purpose of the speech/action. Throw off the love of praise in indifferent particulars (dress, small perfections); be indifferent where proper so great qualities are not robbed by attention to trifles. Beware affectation in conversation, premeditated speeches, at the Bar, and even in the Pulpit (avoid impertinent wit, quaint phrases, and self-becoming humility that preserve an 'air'). Example anti-patterns: searching for applause in trivial gestures, prearranged facial contortions to display teeth, theatrical adjusting of clothes to attract notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer blank verse for English tragedy; avoid rhyme and mixing modes
rubrics_metrics.description: English blank verse is the most proper for Tragedy because it lifts discourse above prose while remaining close to ordinary speech; a play in rhyme is as absurd in English as hexameters would be in Greek.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use blank verse as the default medium for tragedy. Avoid mixing rhyme and blank verse within the same play (this is like using two different languages). Limited exceptions allowed: concluding a Tragedy or an Act with two or three couplets to function like an aria after recitative, or brief hemistichs/abrupt pauses when they suit passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let ornamented language obscure thought; prioritize sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Our English poets often succeed better in style than in sentiments; the language may be noble and sonorous while the sense is trifling or common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a noble thought expressed in plain language to a vulgar thought swelled by pompous expression. To ensure the thought is sufficiently great or natural for the speaker, lay down dialogue in plain English before turning it into verse and, as a reader, consider the naked thought of each speech divorced from its ornamental phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match expression complexity to function; avoid elaborate phrasing in passionate parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions ought to be much laboured in the unactive parts of the fable (descriptions, similitudes, narrations), but pompous phrases, hard metaphors, and forced expressions often obscure the opinions, manners and passions of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve elaborate, laboured expression for descriptive and narrative passages; keep language of represented passions, opinions, and manners clear so the sentiment is not hidden by 'smoak' of words. Example anti-pattern: using inflated metaphors for a passionate speech that should move by plain force of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft dialogue in plain prose before versifying
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful corrective is for the writer to lay down the whole contexture of his dialogue in plain English before he turned it into Blank Verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write scenes and speeches in straightforward prose first to test the naturalness and strength of thought; after that, versify, ensuring the verse does not introduce false grandeur that masks weak ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow metrical irregularities where passion requires them (hemistichs, pauses)
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not dislike Speeches that close with an Hemistick or abrupt Pauses and Breakings-off in the middle of a Verse, when they humour any Passion that is expressed by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hemistichs, abrupt pauses, and variety of numbers to avoid monotony and to reflect passion authentically. Employ such irregularities deliberately to serve emotional truth rather than as mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not demand poetic justice; unhappy endings can be more effective
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern notion that virtuous characters must be delivered out of their troubles (equal distribution of rewards and punishments) has no foundation in nature or in the practice of the ancients; tragedies that end unhappily often produce stronger terror and commiseration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the ending (happy or unhappy) according to its effect on the audience and the truth of the fable. Avoid mechanically forcing virtue to triumph to satisfy a critical doctrine; tragic impact may be heightened when virtue sometimes suffers or is miserable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tragi-comedy and double plots unless the under-plot supports the main design
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragi-Comedy is a monstrous invention that mixes mirth and sorrow; double plots divert grief to another object, weakening concern for the principal action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not weave disparate tones or a second plot that distracts from primary tragic action. If an under-plot is used, ensure it bears a near relation to the principal design and is concluded by the same catastrophe so it contributes to, rather than dilutes, the main tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rants and bombast (vehemence for applause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain warm and passionate parts are magnified into 'rants'—vehemence added where there is no passion, swelling into bombast; unnatural exclamations, curses, vows, blasphemies, and defiance pass for towering thoughts and gain applause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write passionate speech from genuine feeling, not to elicit a theatrical clap. Do not inflate language merely to create a dramatic moment; bombast may please ill taste but undermines true greatness. Example anti-pattern: adding grandiose exclamations that are not supported by the scene's thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware inconsistent characterization to please particular audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors often make heroes insolent to men and abject to women to recommend them to the fair part of the audience—an artifice that pleases but may be inauthentic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid designing character behaviour solely as a device to charm subsets of the audience. Strive for consistent character motivation; do not alternate proud affronts and abject submissions purely as a crowd-pleasing trick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match register to the fable's nature (domestic vs grand subjects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets like Otway follow Nature in language and therefore shine in passionate parts, especially where the fable is familiar and domestic; but such familiarity can be too much where dignity is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use familiar, natural language for domestic or intimate fables to achieve tenderness and force. For grand, dignified subjects, raise the style appropriately so that important parts have elevated expression in keeping with Aristotle's rule about fitting expression to function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of numbers and occasional changes of metre to avoid weariness
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a Diversity of Numbers in some Parts of the Old Tragedy, in order to hinder the Ear from being tired with the same continued Modulation of Voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce occasional changes in rhythm and metre (diverse numbers) to refresh the ear across a long performance. This can include brief lyric passages, hemisticks, or other variations used judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of appearance and expression (natural vs painted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural faces show lively, animated aspect; painted faces (cosmetic 'borrowed complexions') have dead, uninformed countenances that do not display the swell of muscles with passion or surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer natural, expressive appearances in persons and characters; beware of artificial appearances that conceal real expression. As a social rule, authenticity (in face, voice, and manner) reveals feeling and character; painted or fixed appearances mask those qualities and are judged as counterfeit.
